text: Question thirteen. What is the difference between a measure and a metric? A measure is a raw aggregate on one table, like the sum of amount. A metric is the business number built from measures, with filters, ratios or time logic, like completed revenue. Question fourteen. What does a metric definition contain? The aggregation, the entity and grain it lives on, the dimensions it can be sliced by, its filters, and its time grain. A ratio adds a numerator and a denominator. Question fifteen. What is the difference between additive, semi-additive, and non-additive metrics? Revenue sums across everything. An account balance sums across accounts but not across months: take the latest, or the average. Ratios and distinct counts never sum; recompute them from the rows. Question sixteen. What is governance in the metrics context? An owner for each metric, code review on every change, certification of the trusted ones, documented meaning and lineage, and access controls. Question seventeen. What is a cumulative or time-window metric, and why define it centrally? It aggregates over a trailing window, like rolling twenty-eight-day active users, or month-to-date revenue. Windows are easy to get subtly different by hand, so define the grain and the window once. Question eighteen. When is a wide, pre-joined mart preferable to querying through a semantic layer? For a heavy BI workload, or a tool that struggles with dynamic joins: reads are fast and predictable. It costs flexibility and storage, and its logic must still come from the governed definitions, or it becomes one more place to drift. All of these definitions were written for people reading dashboards. Now the reader is a language model. Next: AI and the semantic layer.
